sections.normalized_html: In a right triangle [MATH: \triangle MNO,] the sum of the measures of angles [MATH: \angle M] and [MATH: \angle N] is [MATH: 90^\circ.] If [MATH: \cos(m\angle M) = \dfrac{16}{25},] what is the value of [MATH: \sin(m\angle N)?]
sections.readable_text: In a right triangle [MATH: \triangle MNO,] the sum of the measures of angles [MATH: \angle M] and [MATH: \angle N] is [MATH: 90^\circ.] If [MATH: \cos(m\angle M) = \dfrac{16}{25},] what is the value of [MATH: \sin(m\angle N)?]

sections.normalized_html:
In any right triangle, the two non-right angles are complementary. Since triangle [MATH: \triangle MNO] is a right triangle, angles [MATH: \angle M] and [MATH: \angle N] must satisfy [MATH: m\angle M + m\angle N = 90^\circ.]

Therefore, [MATH: m\angle N = 90^\circ - m\angle M.] Hence, [MATH: \sin(m\angle N) = \sin(90^\circ - m\angle M).]

Using the trigonometric identity [MATH: \sin(90^\circ - \theta) = \cos\theta,] we find that [MATH: \sin (m∠N)|= \sin (90^{∘} − m∠M); = \cos (m∠M).]

We are told [MATH: \cos(m\angle M) = \dfrac{16}{25}.] So, it follows that [MATH: \sin(m\angle N) = \dfrac{16}{25}.]

items.title: Simplifying an Expression With Cofunction Identities

sections.normalized_html:
Which of the following expressions is equivalent to

[MATH: (\sin 12^\circ)(\cos 78^\circ) + (\cos 12^\circ)(\sin 78^\circ)?]

  1. [MATH: (\sin 12^\circ)^2 + (\cos 12^\circ)^2]

  2. [MATH: \sin 12^\circ + \cos 12^\circ]

  3. [MATH: 2(\sin 12^\circ)^2]

  4. [MATH: 2(\cos 12^\circ)^2]
sections.readable_text:
Which of the following expressions is equivalent to

[MATH: (\sin 12^\circ)(\cos 78^\circ) + (\cos 12^\circ)(\sin 78^\circ)?]

1. [MATH: (\sin 12^\circ)^2 + (\cos 12^\circ)^2]
2. [MATH: \sin 12^\circ + \cos 12^\circ]
3. [MATH: 2(\sin 12^\circ)^2]
4. [MATH: 2(\cos 12^\circ)^2]

sections.normalized_html:
First, notice that all the answer choices only involve trigonometric functions of [MATH: 12^\circ.] So, we need to rewrite the original expression entirely in terms of [MATH: 12^\circ.]

Since [MATH: 78^\circ = 90^\circ - 12^\circ,] we can do this with the cofunction identities [MATH: \sin(90^\circ - \theta) = \cos\theta, \qquad \cos(90^\circ - \theta) = \sin\theta.]

Replacing every instance of [MATH: 78^\circ] with [MATH: 90^\circ - 12^\circ,] we have

[MATH: (\sin 12^\circ)(\cos (90^\circ - 12^\circ)) + (\cos 12^\circ)(\sin (90^\circ - 12^\circ)).]

Applying the cofunction identities, the expression becomes

[MATH: (\sin 12^\circ)(\sin 12^\circ) + (\cos 12^\circ)(\cos 12^\circ)] which we can write as

[MATH: (\sin 12^\circ)^2 + (\cos 12^\circ)^2]

which further simplifies to [MATH: 1] by the Pythagorean identity.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:

Content:
In this topic, we’ll practice recognizing and applying cofunction relationships to simplify trigonometric expressions and solve for missing values.

Item 2 — Example: Determining Sine and Cosine Given the Cofunction of the Complementary Angle

Example Prompt:
In a right triangle [MATH: \triangle MNO,] the sum of the measures of angles [MATH: \angle M] and [MATH: \angle N] is [MATH: 90^\circ.] If [MATH: \cos(m\angle M) = \dfrac{16}{25},] what is the value of [MATH: \sin(m\angle N)?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
In any right triangle, the two non-right angles are complementary. Since triangle [MATH: \triangle MNO] is a right triangle, angles [MATH: \angle M] and [MATH: \angle N] must satisfy
[MATH: m\angle M + m\angle N = 90^\circ.]

Therefore, [MATH: m\angle N = 90^\circ - m\angle M.] Hence,
[MATH: \sin(m\angle N) = \sin(90^\circ - m\angle M).]

Using the trigonometric identity
[MATH: \sin(90^\circ - \theta) = \cos\theta,]
we find that
[MATH: \sin (m∠N)|= \sin (90^{∘} − m∠M); = \cos (m∠M).]

We are told [MATH: \cos(m\angle M) = \dfrac{16}{25}.] So, it follows that
[MATH: \sin(m\angle N) = \dfrac{16}{25}.]
